newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK's Hang Lung Group buoyant on 1996 prospects.
newsitem.headline: HK's Hang Lung Group buoyant on 1996 prospects.

text.p: Hong Kong's Hang Lung Group said on Friday it has survived a difficult period for property investment, and is now ready to ride the back of improving consumer sentiment.
The group's investment arm, Hang Lung Development Co Ltd, announced its net profits surged more than five percent, and said a retail rent recovery had already begun.
"Retail rents have begun to recover," said Ronnie Chan, chairman of the Hang Lung Group, in a statement.
"Consumer sentiment is much better than a year ago. Both prices and rents for high end residential properties have done very well."
Hang Lung Development is an investment holding company that also has interests in property investment and development, hotels, department stores and restaurants.
The company announced on Friday that its net profit for the year ended June 30, 1996, was HK$2.2 million, an increase of 5.3 percent compared with the previous year.
The property investment arm of the Hang Lung Group, Amoy Properties Ltd, announced a 2.1 percent increase in net profits over the previous year despite fluctuations in the property market.
"The past year has been a very difficult period for property investment," Chan said. "The company has nevertheless managed to grow rental income slightly."
As consumer sentiment improved in Hong Kong, so would prospects for this year, he said.
"In the past few months, consumer spending in Hong Kong has improved somewhat.
"Although this has not yet been translated into rental increases, I believe we can now see light at the end of the tunnel. As consumer sentiment improves, we can expect rents to firm up," he said.
Grand Hotel Holdings Ltd, the group's hotels subsidiary, announced a significant increase in net profit of 39 percent.
"Thanks to the strong hotels market, we were able to raise room rates, while achieving high occupancy levels," Chan said.
"Lower inflation of late has also contained operating expenses resulting in better oeprating margins."
During the year the average occupancy rate for the hotel industry in Hong Kong improved by three percent over the previous year to 87 percent, he said.
